fix(messaging): stop messages getting stranded in processing

A message sits at 'processing' from the moment it is enqueued until the
worker writes a terminal status. Any error in between stranded it there
for good: a failed job is rejected to a dead-letter list rather than
redelivered, and delete was blocked on that state.

An unreadable message document was the common trigger. It fell through
with every attribute unset, so the provider lookup rejected a null type
and aborted the job with a misleading query error.

- guard the message read in the worker
- mark a message failed when the job dies before writing a status
- allow deleting a processing message so stranded ones can be cleared

fix(messaging): keep a terminal status when cleanup fails

Delivery is followed by attachment cleanup, which throws on its own when
a bucket or file backing an attachment is gone. Reaching the fallback
with a status already written rewrote a delivered message to failed and
attributed a storage error to it, while it kept its delivery count and
timestamp.

Skip the fallback write once the message holds a terminal status.

Add opt-in spread for scheduled function enqueues

Cron schedules cluster on shared slots (everyone runs `0 * * * *`), so
the scheduler enqueued every same-slot execution in the same second — a
thundering herd of simultaneous invocations and runtime cold starts at
the top of the hour.

When _APP_FUNCTIONS_SCHEDULE_SPREAD is set to N seconds, each function
gets a deterministic offset (abs(crc32(functionId)) % N) added to its
enqueue delay. Functions keep a stable slot so run intervals stay exact,
and enqueue-delay telemetry measures against the intended (spread) time.
Default is 0: behavior is unchanged.

(chore): bump docker-base to 2.0.0

2.0.0 fetches every PHP extension by commit SHA and verifies the PECL
tarball by checksum, so the base is no longer assembled from mutable
upstream tags, and it carries the extension updates that came with that
(swoole 6.2.2, mongodb 2.3.3, protobuf 5.35.1, zstd 0.17.0, xdebug 3.5.3
and the rest) on a freshly patched php:8.5-alpine.

It also stops shipping XDebug in the default tag. That was never
intentional — docker-base's Dockerfile ended with the XDebug stage and
its build passed no --target, so the debugger rode along into the image
Appwrite and Cloud both build on. This repo depended on that accident:
the development target copies dev/xdebug.ini, which is
`zend_extension=xdebug`, but nothing here ever installed the extension.

XDebug now comes from the 2.0.0-xdebug tag, which is the same base build
with the extension added, so the module API always matches. It is mounted
rather than copied, so xdebug.so only enters a layer when DEBUG=true, and
only in the development stage — production has no path to it. Verified:
production and Cloud images report no xdebug module and no xdebug.so,
`--target production` never builds the xdebug stage at all, and
`--target development --build-arg DEBUG=true` loads Xdebug 3.5.3.

The XDebug removals in the base and production stages went with it. They
existed to strip what the base wrongly shipped, and now strip nothing.

fix(databases): support text, varchar and format column types inline

Creating a table/collection with its schema in one call rejected every
non-legacy string type. The shared Attributes validator's supported-type
list was never updated when the text/varchar family was introduced, so

request and had to fall back to createTable + N column calls.

consume it from both the validator and the inline attribute builder, so

again. The format shorthands (email, url, ip, enum) are now accepted as
a `type` too, mirroring createEmailColumn and friends, and a string with
an explicit `format` no longer needs a `size`.

test(migrations): budget the migrated function's cold start, and name it when it loses

The migrated function's first execution in the destination project is a guaranteed
cold start, and the function's timeout is the executor's WHOLE budget rather than
the time its code gets: it is passed straight through as `timeout:` and the
executor spends it creating the container and booting node before the handler
runs. This fixture never set one, so it inherited the 15s API default and the
migration copied that to the destination. Ten seconds was already measured as too
little for a cold start on CI's docker-in-docker daemon, so 15 has almost no
margin over the same cost.

What that costs is invisible, which is the second half of this change. When the
executor throws, the sync execution endpoint records status `failed` with the
reason in `errors`, leaves `logs` empty, and -- because an ExecutorException is
not an AppwriteException -- returns 201 anyway. The assertion pinned only the
logs, so the run reported `Failed asserting that '' contains "body-is-test"` and
said nothing about whether the execution failed, timed out, or merely lost its
logs. Asserting the status first, with the body in every message, makes the next
occurrence name its own cause.

The logs assertion stays one-shot on purpose: retrying until logs appear would
also swallow a genuine logs-loss regression, which is the one thing here worth
failing over.

Filter model-typed rules handed raw arrays

output() recursed into a rule's items only when they were already Documents,
so an endpoint passing config rows straight through shipped every key on
them. listFrameworks did exactly that and leaked each adapter's startCommand
along with the framework-level bundleCommand, envCommand and screenshotSleep.

Coerce arrays to Documents where the rule names a model, which lets the
declared rules govern the output wherever the payload came from, and drop
the wrapping listFrameworks needed to work around it.

A union type is always a list of models, never scalars, so the array check
is enough to tell a nested model from a rule like runtimes.

fix(sites): leave the TanStack Start static directory alone

Drops the TanStack half of this change, leaving only the Nuxt path.

The invariant covers every framework, so reverting the directory on its
own turns the suite red on tanstack-start: a nitro ssr directory beside a
vite-native static one is exactly what the rule rejects. Skip that
framework while the layout question is open, and the check keeps guarding
the Nuxt path and everything else.

Coerce only single model rules, never unions

Coercing a union-typed value into a Document reached a branch that had
never run: the single-value path hands rule['type'] to output(), which
takes a string, so a user's hashOptions returned a 500 instead of its
algo. Only the array branch resolves a model per item.

Restrict the coercion to array rules naming one model, and leave the
single-value path as it was.

chore: bump messaging to 2.1 and drop PHPMailer

utopia-php/messaging 2.1.0 sends over utopia-php/smtp, so PHPMailer is no
longer pulled in with it. The one place we used it directly was the
project SMTP endpoint, which builds a mailer only to find out whether the
configuration works -- it never sends anything through it.

That check is now a client that reports what the server offers, which is
the same conversation: greet, upgrade if asked for, authenticate. Failure
still surfaces as PROJECT_SMTP_CONFIG_INVALID carrying the reason, and
now the reason is the server's own reply rather than "Connection is not
valid."

Behaviour is unchanged for every configuration that mattered, checked
against a real server both ways:

  no auth, no encryption   valid       PHPMailer: valid
  good credentials         valid
  wrong password           invalid     535 5.7.8, quoted from the server
  nothing listening        invalid     connection refused
  self-signed certificate  invalid     PHPMailer: invalid

The last row is the one worth naming: neither accepts a certificate the
system does not trust, so a server that was refused before is still
refused, with a clearer explanation.

refactor(schedules): run the schedulers on utopia-php/schedule

The three scheduler tasks shared a base class that hand-rolled the loop, and
that loop lost runs two ways. It recomputed a fresh look-ahead window from the
moment each tick started while evaluating every cron against a moving "now",
so the wall time the pass itself consumed became an interval no window
covered, and any occurrence landing there was skipped permanently — no error,
no execution record, no retry. It also held no watermark, so everything due
while the process was down was lost outright. Both are why a customer's
*/15 function has been missing runs, and neither was reachable by a test: the
window arithmetic and the clock were tangled into the same method.

utopia-php/schedule owns that arithmetic now. Occurrences come from explicit
half-open windows that tile — each opens exactly where the previous committed
one closed — and a window is committed only after its occurrences have been
handed over, so a tick that dies repeats rather than skips. The committed
window travels with the leadership claim in one Redis compare-and-swap, which
also means replicas of a scheduler elect a single dispatcher, a replacement
resumes coverage where its predecessor stopped, and a deposed leader's late
commit is fenced instead of rewinding coverage.

ScheduleBase is gone rather than reimplemented: each task now constructs its
own scheduler, so what it schedules and how it dispatches read top to bottom
in one file. What the three genuinely share — paging the schedules collection
for a region and resource type, resolving projects, loading resources,
dropping orphans — is a collaborator, ScheduleSource, not an inherited
template. Each task supplies the two things that differ: how to load its
resource, and what its stored schedule attribute means. Functions read it as a
cron expression, executions and messages as a fixed moment, which is also how
one-shots now retire: the library drops them once delivered.

Behaviour held constant on purpose. Functions keep the deterministic spread
offset and still sleep to the exact second, so runs land where they always
did; executions keep their four-second lead time; messages take none at all,
because a message must never go out early. Recovered past-due runs clamp to
zero delay instead of sleeping a negative interval, and catch-up is bounded by
a lookback so a long outage replays a capped burst rather than everything since
it began.

The claim store borrows from the lock pool rather than the legacy `redis`
resource. That resource reads _APP_REDIS_HOST, which deployed environments
leave unset — it would have resolved to localhost, and a scheduler that cannot
take its claim never dispatches at all. The lock pool is built from
_APP_CONNECTIONS_LOCKS, which they do set, and borrowing per call lets the
pool replace a connection that dies instead of stranding the claim.

Tests cover what this repository still owns: that each task reads its schedule
attribute as the right kind of trigger, that an unusable cron expression is
rejected once where the row is built rather than silently matching nothing
forever, and that only the tasks which sleep take lead time. The window
tiling, watermark and failover behaviour are covered by the library's own
suite, which replays this incident's tick phase over an hour and asserts every
occurrence is delivered exactly once.

Requires a lockstep change in appwrite/cloud: ScheduleBackups extends the
deleted base class, so it needs its own scheduler the same way these three now
have theirs. Cloud's other three subclasses keep working — spreadWindow and
updateProjectAccess are still there for them to override.

Rebased onto the combined worker and scheduler work that landed meanwhile, so
each task keeps the lifecycle that container drives: setup() wires the
publisher and telemetry, start() builds the scheduler and loads the schedules
once (serially, so resource types do not contend for the shared console and
cache pools), and listen() runs the loop in its own coroutine. The library's
sleeps yield under the runtime hooks app/cli.php already enables, so three
loops share one process. A test pins those four signatures, because drift in
them would otherwise only surface when the combined container boots.

refactor(schedulers): record project access on consume, not on publish

The schedulers hand over a due second's occurrences one at a time, so the
access write sat on the critical path: every later occurrence in the same
second waited for it. In one production region that loop reaches ~110
occurrences in a single second, and the platform-database round trip is
roughly half the per-occurrence cost.

The functions worker already holds the project and the platform database, and
processes many messages at once, so it is the cheaper place to record it. It
was already doing so for the scheduled-execution republish path; that call
moves up to cover every message instead, which also means an execution counts
as access however it was triggered rather than only when a scheduler published
it.

ScheduleMessages keeps its own call: the messaging worker has no
dbForPlatform injection, so there is nowhere yet to move it to.

Access is now recorded when the execution is processed rather than when it is
enqueued, so a backed-up queue records it late. It is best-effort billing
metadata, which is why the write is throttled in the first place.

Also adds occurrence attributes to every scheduler's enqueue span — due time,
lateness, and the position and size of the batch being handed over. Diagnosing
the region above meant reconstructing burst size and position from log
timestamps; these make that a query.

fix(specs): keep open enums open in the generated spec (#13295)

* fix(specs): keep open enums open in the generated spec

A param declared as `AnyOf([WhiteList(...), Text(...)])` accepts any string
at runtime — the whitelist names the values callers usually want and the text
branch keeps everything else valid. The formatter resolved such a union by
taking `getValidators()[0]` and discarding the rest, so the text branch never
reached the spec. Paired with an `enum:` declaration the result advertises a
closed set for a param that is deliberately open, and generated SDKs then
reject values the endpoint would have accepted.

Emit the union the way OpenAPI already expresses it, with `anyOf` over the
enum branch and a plain string branch. That mirrors the validator exactly, so
a generator can widen the parameter type while still offering the enum for
discovery, and it needs no new vendor extension — the enum branch carries the
same `x-enum-name` / `x-enum-keys` it does today.

Strictness is derived from the validator rather than declared separately, so
it cannot drift from what the endpoint actually accepts — that drift is what
produced the wrong spec in the first place.

No committed spec changes: the union is only emitted when an open union also
declares an enum, and no param in this repository does both.

* refactor(specs): simplify open enum handling

* test(specs): focus open enum coverage

analytics storage take down the core API. The gating was inconsistent
too: only the dev override waited on the one-shot, so in the shipped
compose it was an orphan sitting at Exited (0), which reads as a failure.

Call Connection::setup() from the existing boot block instead. It retries
on the same 15x2s ladder as the databases above so a cold start wins the
race against ClickHouse, then gives up with a warning rather than
blocking boot. Reads and ingestion already gate on Connection::isReady(),
so both stay correct while the schema is missing.

Keep bin/usage-setup and the CLI task -- they repair a dropped table
without a restart, the closest analogue to Cloud's manual script -- and
put its retry on the same ladder.

* refactor(usage): open the read endpoints for edition-specific policy

Cloud has to enforce plan history limits, the premium geo addon, and its
affiliate metric carve-out on the same two endpoints, and today it does
that by keeping a full copy of both actions. The copies have already
drifted behind this branch's gauge fixes, so the duplication is actively
losing correctness rather than merely costing lines.

Make the upstream actions subclassable instead:

- widen the dimension/filter/interval constants and the query helpers from
  private to protected
- read them through `static::` so an override actually takes effect --
  `self::` binds to the defining class and would silently ignore Cloud
- inject a `usagePolicy` object the actions consult before querying. The
  self-hosted implementation allows everything, since self-hosted has no
  plans, addons, or reseller namespaces. Cloud binds a subclass that
  carries the checks its endpoints do today.

The policy is injected rather than hung off the action because actions are
shared across coroutines, so per-request state cannot live on `$this`.

Also fold `country` filters through Context::normalizeCountry() on the way
in. Writes have always stored the column lowercased, readers did not fold
the filter, and ClickHouse compares case-sensitively -- so
`equal("country", ["US"])` returned an empty series. Both sides now share
one rule, with a unit test pinning them together.

Cloud opens its first window at `_APP_STATS_RESOURCES_INTERVAL` unfloored,
so an interval below the 300s bucket size yields a window that closes
before any whole bucket has elapsed and samples nothing at all.

Cloud's container does not define, and inject() is positional and cannot be
dropped by a subclass. The fold is a well-defined domain concept and takes
only a Usage instance, so it becomes Appwrite\Usage\Concurrency and both

refactor(functions): fetch variables fresh for scheduled executions

The scheduler kept the full function document, variables included, in
its in-memory snapshot, and the worker executed scheduled runs from
that snapshot. Variable CRUD therefore had to bump the schedule row's
resourceUpdatedAt so the scheduler would re-read the function — and
project-level variables, which never bumped it, went stale until an

fix(usage): contain per-cycle failures in the stats-resources loop

An exception thrown inside the Console::loop closure ends the loop. The
process does not exit, so a container restart policy never fires, and with no
liveness probe nothing observes that scheduling has stopped: the task keeps
reporting healthy while queueing nothing.

That is not theoretical. A single transient timeout on the usage-store read at
the top of the closure ended gauge collection for an entire region. The task
stayed up and idle for weeks -- 22 log lines total, none after the failure --
until someone noticed the numbers had stopped moving in the console.

Two changes:

  - Wrap the cycle body. Any failure now costs one interval, not the process.
    The next tick retries in full.

  - Stop letting concurrency sampling gate project scheduling. The sample reads
    the usage store; the scheduling scan reads the platform DB. They share no
    data, so a failure in the first has no business preventing the second. It
    is now caught separately and the scan proceeds.

An unready usage schema also becomes a skipped cycle with a logged error
rather than a RuntimeException out of the loop, which had the same terminal
effect as any other throw.

Verified against both revisions with the closure driven directly: on main a
throwing sample() escapes and queues 0 projects; with this change it is
contained, logged, and all projects are still queued.

fix(http): probe the database in the loop that waits for it

createDatabase() waits for a database to accept connections by building its
handle in a try/catch and retrying. Building a handle used to dial, because
setting a timeout on a pooled adapter checked a connection out, so the
construction was the probe the loop was reading - by accident, but reliably.

utopia-php/database 7.2.7 stops that dial, and rightly: a pooled adapter
records a timeout locally and applies it to the SQL it builds, so opening a
connection to set one only meant that building a handle failed while a backing
was unreachable, reporting a database as down to a caller that had issued no
query. On this branch the constraint is ^7.0.0, so the next update takes it.

Once it does, this loop breaks on its first pass against a database that is
still starting and its warning can never fire. Nothing breaks today - the
create() retry below catches the connection error and waits there instead -
but the wait has moved to a different loop with a different budget, and the
one written for the job stopped doing it. Ask for a connection here.

feat(jobs): join the success path on build distribution

A build that has to exist somewhere other than the region that produced it was
copied out from inside finalize(), which runs under jobs-deployment:<id>. Cloud's
override waits for every edge to report the build available, up to 60s, so the
lock was held across it: other callbacks for that deployment get 10s to acquire
and could never win, and the 30s lease lapsed mid-copy, dropping mutual
exclusion. Successful spans of 34s, 35s and 82s were all present in one
12-minute production window.

The wait belongs between callbacks, not inside one. Three seams, all no-ops
here because a self-hosted build is servable in the only place it exists:

- dispatchDistribution() starts the copies, called once the build is known good
  — joined, detected, artifact present, within the size limit — so nothing is
  copied that was never going to ship. Called on every retry of the join, so an
  override must be idempotent.
- recordEdgeReady() notes one target answering, driven by the new
  EVENT_EDGE_READY callback rather than by anything this worker polls.
- distributed() gates 'ready' on enough of them having answered, so the status
  never advertises a deployment some region cannot serve.

Each report re-enters through onEdgeReady() and retries the join, so the
terminal write happens in a callback of its own, holding the lock only as long
as the write takes.

feat(jobs): join the success path on build distribution

A build that has to exist somewhere other than where it was produced was copied
out from inside finalize(), which runs under jobs-deployment:<id>. Downstream
that copy waits on other systems — Appwrite Cloud fans a site build out to every
edge and waits for each to report it available, bounded only by its own 60s poll
timeout. Two consequences, both observed in production:

- Starvation. Other callbacks for that deployment get LOCK_TIMEOUT (10s) to
  acquire, so across a 60s hold none can win. They are destroyed, not delayed,
  including the sibling half of the success join.
- Lost mutual exclusion. LOCK_TTL is 30s, so a 60s copy structurally outlives
  the lease and another coroutine can enter the critical section.

One 12-minute window held successful spans of 34s, 35s and 82s against a ~150ms
median.

The waiting belongs between callbacks, not inside one. Two seams, both no-ops
here because a build is servable in the only place it exists:

- dispatchDistribution() starts the copies, called once the build is known good
  — joined, detected, artifact present, within the size limit — so nothing is
  copied that was never going to ship. Called on every retry of the join, so an
  override must be idempotent.
- distributed() gates 'ready' on enough copies having arrived, so the status
  never advertises a deployment that cannot be served.

How a copy reports back is not this class's business, so it holds no vocabulary
for it. The default match arm becomes onCallback(): a worker that puts its own
events on this queue handles them there, with the deployment read and the lock
held, and the outcome is published like any other callback's. An unrecognised
callback returns the deployment untouched rather than erroring — it belongs to
something this class does not know about.

feat(jobs): let the ready transition be deferred

finalize() runs under jobs-deployment:<id>, and a downstream worker with work to
do before a deployment may be published did it there. Appwrite Cloud copies a
site build out and waits for the result, bounded only by its own 60s timeout, so
the lock was held across it: other callbacks for that deployment get
LOCK_TIMEOUT (10s) to acquire and could never win, and LOCK_TTL (30s) is shorter
than the wait, so the lease lapsed and mutual exclusion went with it. One
12-minute production window held successful spans of 34s, 35s and 82s against a
~150ms median.

Waiting belongs between callbacks, not inside one. Two seams, both no-ops here
because a verified build has nothing left outstanding:

- onVerified() runs once the build has passed every check this worker makes, so
  a subclass starts its work at the first point the deployment is publishable and
  not before. Called on every attempt at the transition, so an override must be
  idempotent.
- deferred() holds the transition while that work is unfinished, so 'ready' is
  never published before the deployment can be served.

Neither names what the subclass is waiting for, and this worker has no vocabulary
for it. Whatever it is reports back as its own callback on this queue: the
default match arm is now onCallback(), where a subclass handles events this class
does not define, with the deployment read and the lock held. An unrecognised
callback returns the deployment untouched rather than erroring — it belongs to
something this class does not know about.

fix: keep internal writes working when a migration has not run yet

An attribute added to a collection in app/config/collections is written by the
new code the moment it deploys, but the column only exists once the migration
task has run. Until then every write to that collection threw "Invalid document
structure: Unknown attribute". PR #13326 hit this on identities.photoUrl and
took OAuth2 login down for every provider, which is what #13355 reverted.

The platform, project and logs handles own their schema, so they now drop an
attribute the deployed schema does not have and log a warning instead of
failing the write. The value is lost until the migration runs and the writer
sends it again, which is the same outcome as the feature not being deployed
yet.

Handles for databases and tables the caller owns stay strict: that schema is
theirs, the rejection is the documented 400, and dropping an attribute there
would silently discard data they sent.

have to be bumped together: audit 4.0 and usage 0.15 both require

both require `0.1.*`, so pinning either alone leaves the tree unresolvable.
(`"utopia-php/usage": "^0.14.0"` also excludes 0.15.0 on its own — Composer's
caret on a 0.x version only allows the patch range.)

The usage endpoints follow the enum: `VALID_FILTER_METHODS` holds `Method`
cases, and `parseFilterQueries()` compares against them directly. The old

Use Utopia query builder for executions

Refuse variable keys that are invalid env var names

Variable keys become container env var names at build and runtime. A key
holding a stray tab or UTF-16 bytes (e.g. a .env file saved as UTF-16 and
imported, storing every character with an interleaved NUL byte) passed
the plain length check, was stored, and then invalidated the build job
manifest at submission - failing every deployment for that resource with
an opaque internal error.

Two layers, two rules:

- Endpoint guard: the new VariableKey validator on the function, site and
  project variable create/update endpoints requires a C_IDENTIFIER, so
  every accepted key is portable to dotenv files, docker --env and POSIX
  shells.
- Build guard: Deployments::variables() refuses only what the cluster
  would refuse (apimachinery IsEnvVarName: hyphens and dots allowed), so
  legacy keys like MY-VAR keep deploying, while a key the job would be
  rejected for fails fast with the actual reason written to the
  deployment's buildLogs instead of a generic internal error.

fix(spec): give every parameter a usable example (#13368)

* fix(spec): give every parameter a usable example

Examples in the OpenAPI spec are picked by a switch on the parameter's
validator class. Anything without a case fell through to a default arm that
sets a type and no example, so every generated SDK rendered those parameters
as an empty literal -- `key: ''` rather than `key: '<KEY>'`. 230 parameters
across the three platform specs were affected, `Key` alone accounting for 134
of them through `key`, `newKey`, `column`, `attribute` and `twoWayKey`.

Two causes, fixed together.

Validators with one obviously-correct example now have a case: `Key`,
`ProjectId` and `VariableKey` join `UID` and `Text` on the `<PARAM_NAME>`
placeholder, and `Cron`, `HexColor`, `Domain`, `PublicDomain`, `Hostname` and
`Folder` get a real value each. That covers 147 of the 230 in one place, and
any future parameter built on the same validators.

The rest are context-dependent -- a placeholder cannot serve a numeric bound,
since `<MIN>` is not an integer -- so they carry an explicit `example:` chosen
per use case: column bounds and defaults per column type, `5432` for a
Postgres migration port against `587` for SMTP, scrypt cost parameters, the
`recent()` and `current()` keywords their own defaults already use.

Both `?:` and `!empty()` treat the string "0" as absent, so a declared example
of 0 was discarded in favour of the fallback. Comparing against '' instead
keeps it, which is what makes `min: 0` render on integer columns.

Three parameters still report no example: `file` and `code` on the upload
endpoints, which the generator renders as `InputFile::withPath('file.png')`
rather than a scalar.

* fix(spec): drop the Domain case for a class that does not exist

utopia-php/domains ships ApexDomain and PublicDomain, not Domain, so the case
referenced a class PHPStan could not resolve. The domain validators actually
used by parameters are Utopia\Validator\Domain and
Utopia\Domains\Validator\PublicDomain, both of which keep their case. No
parameter uses ApexDomain, so it stays out.

* fix(spec): keep the enum default inside the documented elements

The enum endpoints reject a default that is not one of the elements, so
documenting `default: 'active'` while `elements` stayed empty produced an
example that fails with `Default value not found in elements` the moment a
caller copies it. Giving elements `["active","inactive"]` makes the pair agree
across all four enum routes.

The two examples are declared on separate ->param() calls with nothing tying
them together, which is how they drifted apart in the first place, so
EnumExampleTest drives each real action and asserts the default it documents
is one of the elements it documents.

* test(spec): drop the enum example test

The elements/default fix stands on its own; the test that pinned their
agreement is removed.

fix(specs): emit valid OpenAPI item types for array parameters

ArrayList copied its inner validator's gettype() name straight into items.type,
so a float list emitted type 'double' - a format, not a type. Any spec carrying
one fails schema parsing, which blocks SDK generation for the whole platform.

fix: persist postgres data by mounting the volume at PGDATA

appwrite/postgres:0.1.0 declares VOLUME /var/lib/postgresql and sets
PGDATA=/var/lib/postgresql/18/docker, but the compose file mounted the
named volume at /var/lib/postgresql/18/data - a sibling of PGDATA, not
PGDATA itself.

Docker therefore satisfied the declared VOLUME with a fresh anonymous
volume on every container creation, and that anonymous volume is where
all Postgres data actually lived. The named appwrite-postgresql volume
stayed empty, so data survived a restart but was discarded by any
container recreate: docker compose down, up --force-recreate, an image
bump, or the documented upgrade entrypoint.

Postgres is the default platform database, so a stock install lost its
console users, projects and data on the first upgrade.

Mount the named volume at /var/lib/postgresql so it covers PGDATA.

fix: warn when upgrade ignores the requested database

The upgrade task accepts --database but always re-derives the engine from
the existing installation and locks it, so the flag was silently
discarded. Someone running `upgrade --database=postgresql` on a 1.9.x
MongoDB install got no indication that the request had been dropped and
that their platform database was still MongoDB.

Default the parameter to an empty string so an explicit value can be told
apart from the default, and warn when it differs from the detected engine.
The warning also states that Appwrite cannot move an existing installation
between database engines, since there is no supported path for it.

Behaviour is unchanged: the detected engine is still what the upgrade uses.

fix: bump APP_CACHE_BUSTER for the 2.0.0 release

APP_CACHE_BUSTER was raised from 4326 to 4327 when this branch was
prepared for 2.0.0, but 1.9.6 had already shipped 4327. The two releases
therefore carried the same value.

The constant is mixed into Request::cacheIdentifier(), so an installation
upgrading from 1.9.6 kept serving responses cached under 1.9.6 keys
instead of invalidating them.

Bump to 4328 so 2.0.0 has a value no earlier release has used.

fix: migrate onboarding and schedule project id in V25

Two console schema changes made since 1.9.6 never reached upgraded
installations. The boot-time sync in app/http.php only creates collections
that do not exist yet, so it skips new attributes on collections that are
already there, and V25 had no case for either one:

- projects.onboarding, written by the API shutdown hook on every matching
  request and read by the console "Get started" checklist. Because the
  platform handle drops unknown attributes, the write was discarded
  silently and the checklist stayed empty forever.
- schedules.projectInternalId and its two indexes, written by
  Projects/Http/Schedules/Create.php on every schedule create.

Add both to V25 using the same guarded style as the surrounding cases, so
re-running the migration warns instead of aborting.

Verified by upgrading a seeded 1.9.6 install to 2.0.0 on MariaDB: both
columns go from absent to present, seeded data survives, and a second
migrate run is a no-op.

fix: make DocumentsDB and VectorsDB connections configurable

DocumentsDB is backed only by MongoDB and VectorsDB only by PostgreSQL,
so an installation that uses either needs that engine reachable. The
connection details were effectively hardcoded:

- docker-compose.yml never listed the _APP_DB_*_DOCUMENTSDB variables, and
  listed no _APP_CONNECTIONS_DATABASE_* variables at all. Compose only
  forwards variables it names, so setting them in .env never reached the
  containers and both pools always fell back to mongodb:27017 and
  postgresql:5432.
- Neither family was described in app/config/variables.php, so the
  installer never wrote them to .env either.
- registers.php read _APP_DB_USER, _APP_DB_PASS and _APP_DB_SCHEMA for both
  pools, so the per-engine credential variables that compose did forward for
  VectorsDB were never consumed.

Forward both families plus the two connection-string overrides on every
service that resolves these pools, describe them in variables.php, and read
the per-engine credentials with a fallback to the shared ones so existing
configurations are unaffected.

appwrite-worker-deletes and appwrite-worker-migrations resolve these pools
too and previously received neither family; they now get both.
appwrite-worker-stats-resources inherits them from appwrite-worker.

Verified on a PostgreSQL installation with no mongodb service: pointing
_APP_DB_HOST_DOCUMENTSDB at a MongoDB reachable under another name makes
DocumentsDB create, write and read back, which was impossible before.

fix: make DocumentsDB and VectorsDB connections configurable

DocumentsDB is backed only by MongoDB and VectorsDB only by PostgreSQL,
so an installation that uses either needs that engine reachable. The
connection details were effectively hardcoded:

- docker-compose.yml never listed the _APP_DB_*_DOCUMENTSDB variables, and
  listed no _APP_CONNECTIONS_DATABASE_* variables at all. Compose only
  forwards variables it names, so setting them in .env never reached the
  containers and both pools always fell back to mongodb:27017 and
  postgresql:5432.
- Neither family was described in app/config/variables.php, so the
  installer never wrote them to .env either.
- registers.php read _APP_DB_USER, _APP_DB_PASS and _APP_DB_SCHEMA for both
  pools, so the per-engine credential variables that compose did forward for
  VectorsDB were never consumed.

Forward both families plus the two connection-string overrides on every
service that resolves these pools, describe them in variables.php, and read
the per-engine credentials with a fallback to the shared ones so existing
configurations are unaffected.

too and previously received neither family; they now get both.
appwrite-worker-stats-resources inherits them from appwrite-worker.

feat: make the database batch limit configurable

APP_LIMIT_DATABASE_BATCH was a hard-coded 100, so bulk row and document
operations rejected anything larger with "Value must a valid array no
longer than 100 items". On Cloud a plan raises it through
databasesBatchSize, but self-hosted had no equivalent lever, leaving

operator owns that trade-off for their own hardware.

feat: let operators choose which database products to deploy

DocumentsDB runs only on MongoDB and VectorsDB only on PostgreSQL, but the
installer provisioned a single engine, the one chosen for the platform. A
default PostgreSQL installation therefore had no MongoDB, so creating a
DocumentsDB database returned 201 and the first collection write failed
with a bare server error, the cause visible only in the logs. A MariaDB
installation lost both products the same way.

Rather than always deploying every engine, ask which products the
installation actually wants:

- _APP_DOCUMENTSDB and _APP_VECTORSDB, both enabled by default, are asked
  during install, seeded from the environment for scripted runs, and
  preserved from the existing .env on upgrade.
- The compose generator adds an engine only when the platform uses it or an
  enabled product needs it, so a deployment runs no database it has no use
  for.
- A disabled product's routes throw GENERAL_SERVICE_DISABLED, for keys and
  privileged roles too, since the engine behind them is not deployed.

Turning a product off now removes its engine instead of leaving an endpoint
that fails on first write.

fix: carry build artifacts across the 2.0 builds volume rename

Before 2.0 the builds volume was declared without a name, so Compose
prefixed it with the project and it became appwrite_appwrite-builds. 2.0
names it explicitly, because jobs-service build containers are created
outside the Compose project and mount it by that literal name through
_APP_BUILDS_VOLUME.

Starting 2.0 on a pre-2.0 installation therefore mounts a new, empty
volume and leaves every existing artifact behind. Deployments stay in the
database looking healthy, pointing at build paths that no longer resolve,
so the executor cannot unpack a source that is not there, never starts a
runtime, and the request fails on the site or function timeout. The only
log line is "Timed out waiting for runtime", which points at the runtime
rather than the missing file, and the first guess tends to be TLS or DNS.

On upgrade, copy a populated <project>_<volume> onto the new volume when
the new one is empty. It copies rather than moves, so the previous volume
remains as a fallback. Nothing happens when the new volume already holds
files, when no previous volume exists, or when more than one candidate
does; the ambiguous case warns and copies nothing rather than guessing.

Volumes are inspected with the Appwrite image, which the upgrade has
already pulled, so this never depends on fetching another image.

fix: migrate builds when the new volume does not exist yet

The guard required the new volume to already exist, but on a real upgrade
it does not: Compose creates it when the containers start, which is after
this runs. Every genuine upgrade therefore returned without copying, and
Compose went on to create the empty volume the migration was meant to
prevent.

Treat only an existing volume that already holds files as "nothing to do".
When the volume is missing, the copy creates it, so the containers attach
to one that already has the artifacts.

refactor: fold the volume helpers into the migration

listVolumes(), volumeExists() and volumeFileCount() were each used only by
the builds migration and only said what a single exec() call already says.

volumeExists() disappears entirely: the listing is fetched anyway, so
membership in it answers the same question without a second docker call.
Counting stays as a local closure, since it is the one step used more than
once. The listing also keeps the count away from volumes that do not exist,
which would otherwise create an empty one as a side effect.

fix: report a partly migrated builds volume instead of skipping

An installation that upgraded once and then rebuilt a single deployment
has files on the new volume while the rest are still on the old one. The
emptiness check treated that as nothing to do, so the remaining artifacts
stayed stranded without a word.

Copying is still the wrong move there, since it would overwrite newer
artifacts with older ones, but the situation should be visible. Warn and
name the volume that still holds files so the operator can copy across
what they need.

refactor(install): make infrastructure migrations versioned

Some upgrades change what the containers run on rather than what is inside
the database: a renamed volume, a moved file, anything the containers depend
on before they can start. Data migrations cannot cover those -- they run
against a database that is already up.

This adds the same shape the request and response filters use for API breaks:
a version-keyed registry, and a range picked with version_compare. Each
release that changes infrastructure gets one class, and an upgrade runs the
classes for the releases it crosses, oldest first. Re-running an upgrade
replays nothing already applied, and a pre-release counts as the release it
leads to so 2.0.0-rc.1 runs what 2.0.0 runs.

The builds-volume copy moves out of Install into V1 as the first of these.
A failed migration warns instead of taking the upgrade down with it.

refactor(install): let a release carry several infrastructure changes

A release rarely changes exactly one thing about what the containers run on.
Version classes now declare their changes as a named list rather than a single
execute(), so each is logged by name and a failure in one does not skip the
rest -- they are independent, and a volume that could not be copied says
nothing about a file that has to move.

getName() becomes the release, and the builds-volume copy becomes the first
change 2.0.0 declares.
docs: simplify the builds volume migration comment
refactor(install): inline the infrastructure migration runner

refactor(install): run docker through Console::execute

Uses the string form: the array form skips the subshell that reports the exit
code back, so every call returns 0 and a failed copy reads as a success.

With exit codes now available, a volume that cannot be read is told apart from
one that is empty. It used to count as empty, which read as nothing to migrate
and stranded the artifacts without a word.

The migration also moves next to the container start it belongs to, so a
resumed upgrade cannot start the containers without it.

fix(install): apply infrastructure changes even with --no-start

They were tied to the container start, so an upgrade that only wrote the new
config left the volume rename unapplied; the operator's own compose up then
mounted an empty builds volume. They now run once the config is written,
which is also the last moment anything can be moved.

fix(install): keep the upgrade source version across a resume

An attempt interrupted after the compose file and .env are rewritten leaves
both reading as the version being installed, so a resumed attempt saw an
upgrade with nothing to cross and started on an empty builds volume.

The source version is now remembered in the installer config before those
files are rewritten, and forgotten once the changes are applied, so a resume
still knows where it started and a completed upgrade never replays.

Writing the installer config also refreshes its cache; a read straight after
a write returned the previous value.

fix(install): keep retry state when an infrastructure change fails

execute() swallowed a failing change, so the upgrade forgot the version it
started from either way and a failed copy could never be attempted again.
It now reports whether everything landed, and the version is only forgotten
once it has.

A change that a later run could still complete raises instead of warning:
volumes that cannot be listed or read, and a copy that does not finish.
Nothing left to do -- no legacy volume, or a target that already holds
artifacts -- stays a warning, since retrying changes nothing.

fix(install): finish a half-done artifact copy instead of giving up

A copy that stopped early -- a full disk, a killed container -- left the new
volume holding some of the artifacts. That looked like a volume someone had
already written to, so the next attempt skipped it, reported success, and
stranded the rest.

The copy now fills in only what is missing, so an artifact rebuilt in the
meantime keeps the newer version and an interrupted copy is carried on rather
than restarted. What is still missing when it finishes is listed and raised,
since a copy can stop early while everything it did run reports success.

Restarting the installer also rewrote its config without the version the
upgrade started from, losing the one record left of it.

A copy killed mid-file leaves a short file behind. Matching on existence

changes have not all landed, whichever step the last attempt reached.

fix(realtime): drop dead fan-out grouping, meter outbound bytes

The fan-out grouped receivers by their matched subscription IDs so one
encoded frame could serve many connections. Those IDs are ID::unique()
per subscription, so no two connections can ever share one and the key
never collapsed -- it built one group of one, every time. Replaced with
a direct loop over $receivers, which says the same thing in fewer lines.

Behaviour is identical: frames, message totals and byte totals are
byte-for-byte equal across 1..1000 connections and 1..3 subscriptions
per connection.

Also meter outbound bytes. Fan-out cost is driven by payload size times
fan-out width, not by message count, and nothing exposed that: during
OnCall #1175 three pods stepped +18/+78/+226Mi at a message rate of
21/s, below a 74/s peek 70 minutes earlier that cost nothing. The
quantity that actually moved was invisible. $outboundBytes was already
computed for usage accounting; this puts it on a counter too.

perf(realtime): single Swoole worker, encode the document once per event

Realtime defaults to one Swoole worker per container instead of
CPU count x _APP_WORKER_PER_CORE (6).

Measured on a single worker holding ~1200 websocket connections: 0.06-0.35
cores, and ~84% of each additional worker's footprint is fixed per-process
overhead rather than connection state (~37MiB fixed vs ~71KiB per
connection). Extra workers also each subscribe to the firehose, so every
worker json_decodes every event, and they split the accept distribution
into a second balancing layer invisible to the deployment (connections per
worker ranged 51-170 inside one container). Concurrency belongs to the
deployment. _APP_WORKERS_NUM still overrides.

Also serialise the event document once per event rather than once per
subscriber. `subscriptions` is the only part of the frame that varies per
connection and it is small, so the rest is encoded once and reused. A
199Hz profile taken during a live fan-out burst put this loop's
json_encode at 26% of on-CPU work, against 2.8% at rest, with 257 of 285
samples on the pubsub callback's encode.

Frames are unchanged apart from key order: 36 comparisons across unicode
escaping, slashes, empty data, nested empties, a pre-set `subscriptions`
key and a blob containing quotes and backslashes all decode identically.

feat: ship DocumentsDB and VectorsDB off by default (#13411)

DocumentsDB runs only on MongoDB and VectorsDB only on PostgreSQL, but an
installation deploys just the engine backing the platform. A default install
therefore had neither engine behind them: creating a database returned 201 and
the first write failed with a bare server error, the cause only in the logs.

Both are now off unless _APP_DOCUMENTSDB or _APP_VECTORSDB says otherwise, and
their routes answer with a service disabled error until then -- to keys and
privileged roles too, since there is no engine to reach either way. Enabling one
means provisioning its engine and pointing the matching _APP_DB_* variables at
it; the installer does not ask, and does not deploy an engine for a product.

fix(proxy): store rule domains in canonical lowercase form (#13417)

The four rule create actions validated the domain with
`Utopia\Validator\Domain`, which does not constrain case, then persisted
the value verbatim — while deriving the rule ID from
`md5(strtolower($domain))`. So a rule created for `MyApp.Example.COM`
stored a domain that did not match the form its own ID was built from.

Downstream that mismatch is not cosmetic: `Utopia\Cdn\Domain::validate()`
treats a non-lowercase domain as malformed, so deleting such a rule threw
and left the certificate row behind. Normalizing on write keeps stored
rows consistent with both the ID derivation and the CDN providers.

test(e2e): give the project-variable function room for a cold start

testProjectVariableInFunction created its function with 'timeout' => 15
and then executed it synchronously, asserting the execution completed.

That timeout is not a handler budget. The executor spends it end to end:
Docker.php bounds the container prepare wait, the launch wait and the
cold-start TCP ping on it, decrementing the remainder after each stage,
and only what survives is left for the function itself. A node-22 cold
start on a contended runner consumes the lot, the executor raises
RUNTIME_TIMEOUT, and the 500 turns the execution status into 'failed'.

The budget was already almost exhausted on the happy path: a passing run
spent 13.76s of the 15s, leaving 1.24s of margin, while a failing run
reached 15.67s and logged "Timed out waiting for runtime." That is the
~20% failure rate this test shows in cloud CI, where it is the only file
in the Project E2E job that creates a function at all.

feat(stats-resources): span each scheduler cycle with its enqueue count

The scheduler logs nothing on its success path -- no per-project enqueue
line, no cycle summary -- so a healthy pod produces no output at all. When
resource gauges stopped arriving for a project, there was no way to tell a
scheduler that had stopped seeing the region from a worker that was dying
on the job; both look identical from Grafana, which is to say invisible.

Wrap the loop body in one span per cycle carrying projects_queued, counted
in the foreachDocument enqueue callback, following the stats-edge task. The
span is finished in a finally so the usage-schema-not-ready early return
still reports itself -- an unfinished span exports nothing, which is the
same blind spot again -- and that path is tagged with a skip reason so a
skipped cycle is not mistaken for a cycle that legitimately queued zero
projects. Console::loop's onError handler finishes the span for anything
that escapes the closure.

Deliberately no first/last sequence fields: they only catch a truncated
cycle and would give false comfort about gaps in the middle of the range.

Ref: DAT-1898

fix(stats-resources): only count enqueues that actually published

The publisher returns false when _APP_USAGE_STATS is disabled and when
publishing threw -- it swallows the exception to keep the scheduler loop
alive and reports it only to Console. Incrementing unconditionally made
projects_queued count those too, which is worse than not counting at all:
the number exists to be a trustworthy denominator for the worker's
completion count, and a region with a broken queue would have reported a
healthy queued count with zero completions, reading identically to a
region whose workers were dying.

Count the false returns separately as projects_failed, so the failures the
publisher currently only writes to Console become queryable alongside the
successes.

fix(vcs): stop the GitHub App installation callback dead-ending

GitHub only echoes the state parameter back when the flow finishes through the
redirect URI. An organisation member requesting owner approval, and an owner
approving that request from GitHub's own settings, both finish on the app's
setup URL instead, which carries no state. The callback then threw a bare 400
whose message blamed the user for being an organisation member -- the check is
only empty($state) and never looks at the caller's GitHub role, so an owner hit
the same page with no way forward.

Authorize now mirrors state into a short-lived, one-shot cookie the callback
falls back to. The error redirect also used a ':' separator instead of '?', so
the console received /settings/git-installations:error=... and could never read
the error back, and empty success/failure values in state overrode the computed
console defaults, turning the remaining failure branch into a bare 400 as well.
The unused setup_action param now distinguishes a submitted request from a
plain permission failure.

fix(vcs): sign the GitHub App installation state

/v1/vcs/github/callback is public and took the projectId and both redirect URLs
straight out of the state parameter, so anyone could name the project an
installation gets attached to, or point the redirect anywhere. The OAuth2
providers already guard this: Authorize/Base signs [projectId, success, failure]
with _APP_OPENSSL_KEY_V1 and Callback/Base fails closed on hash_equals. The
GitHub App flow predates that and was never brought across.

Mirror the same signature into the state Authorize builds and verify it before
the projectId is read. This also covers the fallback cookie, since the cookie
carries the signed state verbatim.

fix(vcs): scope installation repository endpoints to the project

The repository endpoints loaded an installation by id and never checked it
belongs to the requesting project. Authorization does not backstop this: on
admin-mode routes outside /v1/projects*, shared/api.php sets the default
authorization status to false, so getDocument('installations', $installationId)
returns another tenant's document.

Apply the same guard Installations/Get.php, Delete.php and Namespaces/XList.php
already use, so a mismatched project gets INSTALLATION_NOT_FOUND rather than
another tenant's repositories, file contents, branches or detections.

fix(vcs): use the state cookie only when there is no installation to attach

The cookie is set for ten minutes with SameSite=Lax, so a top-level navigation
from another site still sends it. Substituting it for missing state on a request
that carries an installation id let that cookie supply the project for an
installation it was never bound to; the signature covers the project and redirect
URLs, not the installation.

Fall back to the cookie only when there is no installation id, which is the
organisation-member request it exists for. Callbacks that would persist an
installation now require state on the request itself.

fix(vcs): drop the callback state cookie

The cookie guessed that the browser hitting the callback was the one that
started the flow, which SameSite=Lax does not guarantee: any top-level
navigation from another site sent it. Once the callback refused to let it
attach an installation, the only branch it could still reach was the error
redirect, so all it bought was a nicer message on a flow that cannot succeed
anyway -- an organisation member cannot install the app, an owner has to.

It also never helped the case that matters. An owner approving a member's
request from GitHub's settings is a different browser with no cookie, so that
flow needs reconciliation from the installation webhook rather than anything
carried in the request.

Missing state now reports itself plainly in every case.

feat(console): register the console OAuth env vars in .env, compose and docs

The console sign-in credentials were only ever read in app/config/console.php,
so they were absent from the three places every other _APP_* variable is
declared: the committed .env, the appwrite service's environment pass-through,
and the app/config/variables.php registry that documents them.

Without the compose pass-through the variables never reach the container, and
System::getEnv falls back to '' - which surfaces as a live sign-in button that
fails with "provider disabled" and no other diagnostic.

This covers GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket as well as Google. Those three landed
with the same gap and share the block being edited, so splitting them into a
follow-up would touch these exact lines twice.

Only the appwrite service declares them. The console document is built per
request in app/init/resources.php and every read of the provider triple is on
an HTTP path, so no worker or scheduler needs them - unlike _APP_VCS_*, which
build workers do read.

Defaults stay empty and filter stays '' deliberately: Install.php generates a
random value for any empty var whose filter is 'token' or 'password', which
would stamp junk into a fresh install's OAuth client secret.

buildDuration falls back to wall clock since the deployment was created

fix(builds): cap the billed build duration at the build timeout (#13430)

* fix(builds): cap the billed build duration at the build timeout

Jobs::duration() measures wall clock from buildStartedAt, which the first
log callback stamps — so a build that never streamed a line falls back to
the deployment's creation time and measures its whole queue wait. That
value is what Usage\Build::publish() bills, at memory x duration x cpus,
and it is billed for 'failed' exactly as for 'ready'.

The executor backend could not produce this: it measured microtime()
around the build's own execution, so queue wait was structurally
unbillable. Since builds moved to the jobs-service the mean billed
duration of a *failed* build has gone 111s (Jun) -> 157s (Jul) -> 491s
(Aug) while successful builds held at ~52s, and failed builds are now 57%
of all billed build compute fleet-wide.

One production project shows the shape plainly: 2,286 of its 2,311 failed
August builds have buildStartedAt NULL, empty buildLogs, "exit code -1",
and durations at 904-912s. On s-2vcpu-2gb that is ~1.0 GB-hour billed per
build that never ran — 1,869 of its 1,878 billed GB-hours for the month.

Clamp to _APP_COMPUTE_BUILD_TIMEOUT, the same ceiling Deployments hands
the jobs-service as timeoutSeconds: no job outlives it, so nothing past it
can have been build time. Guarded so a 0 or negative value leaves the
measurement alone rather than zeroing every build.

This is a ceiling, not the whole fix — a starved build still bills the
full timeout. Billing 0 when buildStartedAt is NULL, and the build fan-out
that starves them, are follow-ups.

test: stop asserting the weight of a third-party page in testGetScreenshot

testGetScreenshot rendered https://appwrite.io 53 times and asserted the
resulting PNG was larger than 100000 bytes. That is an assertion about the
marketing site's visual design, not about the endpoint. It went red across
every cloud PR on 2026-08-31 when appwrite.io shipped an Init 2.0 splash
screen: the test's cache-buster query makes the request a Cloudflare cache
miss, waitUntil:load snapshots the splash before the page paints, and the
cropped PNG is 10318 bytes. Feeding that render through
Utopia\Image\Image::crop(800, 600) reproduces 10318 byte for byte off CI, so
the failure is the page, not the runner's egress.

Render example.com instead. It is IANA-reserved, carries no JavaScript, and
renders bit-identically across repeated calls and cache-buster queries, which
is why testGetScreenshotComparison already pixel-compares against it and stays
green in the same lane. Assert the output the endpoint actually controls --
that the PNG comes back at the requested 800x600 -- and leave render fidelity
to the pixel comparison that owns it.

The endpoint's SSRF guard rules out an in-cluster target: PublicHostname
rejects any host resolving into a private range and Domain::isKnown() requires
a public suffix, so a hosts override pointing appwrite.io at the test stack
would be refused before the browser is called.

fix: publish build output to the builds device when storage is not local

The jobs-based build system writes the artifact onto the shared builds volume, but the Jobs worker, the executor and the download endpoint all read the deployment's buildPath through the configured storage device. With _APP_STORAGE_DEVICE=s3 the artifact never reached S3, so every build failed with "Build produced no output artifact". With an S3-compatible endpoint (MinIO, etc.) the stored buildPath was also wrong: the device folds the bucket into its root, so the plain volume path pointed at a bucket named "storage".

The deployment now stores the device path as its buildPath (unchanged for the local device), and the Jobs worker moves the artifact off the volume onto a remote device before checking readiness. The separate-profile jobs worker also receives the storage variables it needs to build that device.

fix(databases): list indexes by database and collection sequence, not id

The index list filtered the `indexes` metadata collection on the `databaseId`
and `collectionId` strings while every sibling path (attribute list, the
cursor lookup three lines below, the create-time limit count, and the worker's
delete cascade) keys on `databaseInternalId`/`collectionInternalId`. A
recreated database keeps its id but takes a new sequence, so whenever an
earlier incarnation's index rows outlive it, the list returns them next to the
live ones under the same key.

The 109-point GA campaign hit this on r30 PR-95 (rv109a-vdb-ded, dedicated
VectorsDB): r28 and r29 had left `idx_embeddings` rows at `processing`
(the pool-identity denial fixed in cloud#5573 threw in the worker before
createIndex could mark them `failed`, and the same denial stopped the
delete-database job before its cascade reached them). r30 created the index
cleanly (worker createIndex 0.43s, `available`), the similarity query ranked
correctly, yet the list kept reporting the stale `processing` rows and the row
failed on "index never left processing" for a third round. PR-93 on the same
prefix passed because the attribute list already filters on the sequences.

Both metadata collections carry `_key_db_collection` on the sequence pair, so
the corrected filter is the indexed one.

test(vcs): cover cross-tenant installation isolation end to end

Two console users with their own teams, projects and Gitea accounts: each
connects an installation, neither can use the other's through any of the six
repository endpoints even knowing its id, and the probe by the other tenant's
project id dies on team membership before reaching VCS code. Inviting the
second user into the first team and accepting via the emailed secret makes the

Keep team total in sync with confirmed memberships

Four ways `teams.total` could drift from the confirmed membership rows:

- `Memberships/Delete.php` reused `$membership` for the primary-transfer
  lookup, so the decrement (and the event payload) read the successor
  instead of the deleted membership. When the only remaining member was
  unconfirmed the lookup returned an empty document and the decrement was
  skipped entirely, leaving the team over-counted.
- `Memberships/Create.php` flipped an existing pending membership to
  confirmed on the server side without counting it. Only the branch that
  created a new membership incremented the total.
- `Status/Update.php` checked `confirm` far away from the increment, so two
  concurrent accepts of the same invite both passed the guard and both
  counted. The flip and the increment now share a transaction behind a
  locking re-read, and the loser gets MEMBERSHIP_ALREADY_CONFIRMED.
- `Teams/Create.php` seeded `total => 1` before creating the owner
  membership in a separate statement, so a failure in between left a team
  counting a member that does not exist. Both writes now share a
  transaction.

The Proxy verification tests talk to a resolver the app believes is a public
recursive one. CoreDNS is an authoritative server, so keeping the test zone
self-contained meant regex templates plus catch-all NODATA rules bolted inside
an authoritative zone. Unbound is a recursive resolver: fixtures are one
local-data line per record, redirect zones cover the per-run unique prefixes,
and forwarding is the server's own job. This mirrors deploy/dns-mock in
appwrite-labs/cloud.

Every zone that can answer negatively declares an SOA, because utopia-php/dns
rejects an authoritative NXDOMAIN or NODATA without one and unbound only adds
it when configured.

resolver path, which skips local-zone data and asks the forwarder. On the CI
runner Docker DNS answers any *.localhost with ::1, which is

of failing on the wrong CNAME. An empty authoritative localhost. zone that the
resolver path consults makes every target NXDOMAIN locally, and the wrong

fix(usage): fold realtime concurrency over a trailing window

A realtime worker that stops never emits the closes for its open
connections, so the carried level only ever ratcheted upward: fleet-wide
the gauge read 72,596 against 3,275 live connections, and the peak that
billing takes from it rose 3.7x in five days.

Each bucket is now the net of the deltas inside the trailing
_APP_REALTIME_CONCURRENCY_WINDOW (default 6h). That needs no carried
state and forgets an orphaned open within one window, at the price of
not seeing connections older than the window. 6h was calibrated against
live connection counts per region (fra1 0.86x, nyc3 1.98x, sgp1 1.05x);
shorter hid long-lived connections, longer carried a stopped worker's
opens for the rest of the cycle.

fix(realtime): close a worker's connections when it exits

In process mode the connections belong to the reactor and the registry
that maps them to projects is per worker, so a worker that exits leaves
its connections open; whenever they finally close, onClose runs in a
worker that never registered them and the -1 is skipped. Every rollout,
scale-down and reload therefore added that worker's open count to the
concurrency level for good.

The base adapter exposes no worker-exit hook, so a subclass adds one and
turns on reload_async, which is what makes the hook fire while the loop
is still alive. realtime.php closes every registered connection there,
so the -1, the stats decrement and the presence cleanup all take the
existing onClose path and clients reconnect to a live worker.

fix(usage): stop at a capped read and sample only buckets with deltas

The event read now spans the window as well as the catch-up range, so
it can hit the 50,000-row cap on a long catch-up. The rows come back
time-ascending, so a capped result is still complete for every bucket
before the last one it returned: sample up to there and let the next
run resume, instead of writing levels that are missing deltas and
advancing past them for good.

Sampling every catch-up bucket for any tenant active in the window
multiplied gauge writes for sparse tenants; a tenant is again written
only for the buckets it had deltas in. The window changes the value,
not how often it is sampled.

Wire _APP_REALTIME_CONCURRENCY_WINDOW through variables.php, .env and
the compose services that carry _APP_STATS_RESOURCES_INTERVAL.

fix(usage): make the concurrency window a constant

Only the fold reads it, so it does not need to be an environment
variable or the configuration surfaces that come with one. Like the
interval and the lag, it is a constant; raising it is a code change.

fix(events): generate the attribute event before the action event

`generateEvents()` appended the attribute-qualified pattern after the plain
action pattern for top-level resources, so `users.[userId].update.name`
generated `users.<id>.update` first. Consumers that report a single name read
`events[0]`, so a function triggered by a name change received
`APPWRITE_FUNCTION_EVENT=users.<id>.update` with the attribute dropped.

Sub-resource patterns already emitted the most specific event first; move the
attribute pattern into the same position for top-level resources so `events[0]`
is always the concrete event that happened. This also stops the block emitting
`teams.<id>.update.status` alongside a membership status update -- that event is
not in the events config and the event validator rejects it, so nothing can
subscribe to it.

fix(auth): stop PersonalData from mutating its own state while validating

isValid() lowercased the userId, email, name and phone properties in place
whenever strict mode was off, so the validator carried state from one call
into the next. Lowercase the values into locals instead, leaving the
instance reusable and side-effect free.

fix(vcs): reindex provider pull request ids after removing one

array_diff() keeps the original keys, so untracking a pull request that is
not the last entry leaves a gapped array. providerPullRequestIds is a
declared array attribute, and the structure validator rejects any value that
is not a list, so closing such a pull request threw instead of untracking it.

Reindex at the three call sites that persist the result: the GitHub and Gitea
event handlers, and the shared cleanup used by GitLab and Bitbucket.

Teams membership listing had the same defect through array_filter(), which
also preserves keys. Response::dynamic() writes each entry back to its
original index, so a member with an empty userId in any but the last position
turned the memberships list into a JSON object.

fix(graphql): keep nested payload data past the escaping depth limit

escapePayload() returned null once the depth guard tripped, and the caller
assigns that result straight back into the parent array, so every value below
_APP_GRAPHQL_MAX_DEPTH was replaced with null instead of merely being left
unescaped. Return the payload untouched instead.

Escaping also ran before the recursion, so an array held under a $-prefixed
key was written unrecursed to the escaped key and then restored under the
original key by the recursion step, leaving both keys in the payload. Recurse
first, then escape, so each key is written once.

fix(proxy): skip empty entries in the functions domain list

The guard inside the loop tested the whole comma-separated env string instead
of the current entry, so it could never skip an empty one. With any empty
segment in _APP_DOMAIN_FUNCTIONS - a trailing comma is enough - an empty
hostname reached the domain restriction, and str_ends_with() matches every
value against an empty needle, so every custom domain deeper than an apex was
rejected. The sites loop directly above already checks the loop variable.

fix(databases): emit surface-correct ids in committed transaction events

The commit handler is the only place that builds a row or document event
payload by hand instead of going through processDocument(). It never added the
synthetic $databaseId, which does not exist on a stored document, and wrote
both $tableId and $collectionId unconditionally.

So a function or webhook triggered by a committed transaction received a row
without $databaseId and carrying the legacy $collectionId, contradicting the
Row model. All four surfaces were affected, since the TablesDB, DocumentsDB and
VectorsDB transaction actions extend this one.

Add $databaseId and derive the container key from the group id already
resolved in the same loop, matching processDocument().

fix(databases): restore the column type guard on attribute updates

Both type checks in updateAttribute() closed their parentheses one token early,
so the comparison was evaluated as the argument:

    $attribute->getAttribute(('type') !== $type)

That passes a bool where a key is expected. Without strict_types PHP coerces it
to '1' or '', neither of which is a key on the attribute, so getAttribute()
returned null and the guard never fired - on any of the update endpoints that
funnel through this base.

The result was that updating a column through the wrong type's endpoint, or
changing the filter of a string column, skipped validation instead of returning
column_type_invalid, and handed a mistyped default to the database adapter.

test(functions): pin execution delete to the owning function

The commit written to fix it carried this test and never merged; the correct
form arrived incidentally through an unrelated refactor of the same block, so
the next refactor can drop it again unnoticed.

Deleting through another function's id must 404 and leave the execution intact,
and deleting through the owner must still succeed.

fix(messaging): decrypt email attachments before sending

The messaging worker handed mail adapters the stored file path, which
for a bucket with encryption or compression enabled is ciphertext or
compressed bytes rather than what the recipient should receive. Every
storage read endpoint undoes both transforms before serving; the email
attachment path was the only consumer of stored bytes in the messaging
pipeline that did not.

Attachments are now materialised once per job, ahead of the recipient
fan-out, into a job-unique directory under the project's local uploads
root: decrypt, then decompress, the reverse of what upload applies.
Building them there rather than in buildEmailMessage also stops the work
repeating once per batch per retry attempt, and keeps concurrent
coroutines off a shared destination path. Nothing is written back to the
file's own path, which on a local install is the stored original, so the
DeviceType::Local guards that existed to prevent a self-copy are gone.
Cleanup moves to a finally in action(), covering the failure paths the
old post-delivery block skipped.

A decompressor reports failure as an empty string, so files stored above
the read buffer before 1.5.0 -- which recorded an algorithm they were
never compressed with -- fall back to their stored bytes instead of
being mailed as an empty file. An undecryptable file fails the send.

Attachments carry a path and no content: Sendgrid and Mailgun read only
Attachment::getPath().

fix(messaging): report attachment cleanup that leaves plaintext behind

Recursive delete reports failure by returning false, but so does an
absent directory, which is the normal outcome for a message that
materialised no attachments. Checking the return value alone would flag
almost every send. Test the directory instead: one that is still there
after the delete is decrypted plaintext left on local storage, which
until now went unnoticed because this is the only cleanup and nothing
sweeps the directory afterwards.

Reported through a span rather than thrown, so it cannot bury the
exception the send itself raised.

fix(messaging): fail the send when an attachment cannot be written

Local storage reports a write failure by throwing, but the device
contract allows a falsy return, and an attachment built for a target
that was never written sends the provider after a file that is not
there. Trim three comments that restated the code they sat on.

fix(databases): compare the string guard against the persisted format

Restoring the parentheses alone made the second guard read 'filter', which is

CVE-2026-81525 (high) affects mongodb/mongodb >=2.0.0,<2.4.1; the lock carried
2.1.2. It could not be reached from here: utopia-php/mongo 1.5.3 required
mongodb/mongodb 2.1.*, so the fixed 2.4.1 was outside the constraint and no
update in this repository could take it.

utopia-php/mongo 1.5.4 (utopia-php/mongo#50) removes the requirement rather
than widening it. That package is a from-scratch wire-protocol client and every
MongoDB symbol it names is BSON or a driver exception -- both from ext-mongodb,
not from the composer library -- so the library was installed everywhere and
called nowhere. Widening it instead would have pulled in a package requiring
ext-mongodb ^2.4, which no Appwrite base image ships.

Nothing in this repository referenced the library either: no MongoDB\ symbol
appears anywhere under app/, src/ or tests/, and the only lock entry naming it
is utopia-php/query's require-dev, which is never installed transitively.

Lock moves by exactly two packages, 138 -> 137, nothing added.
`composer audit --locked` now reports no advisories.

fix(usage): page the event read instead of stopping at the row cap

Stopping at the last bucket a capped read completed made no progress
when the cap fell at or before the first bucket awaiting a sample: the
resume point comes from the newest gauge sample, which was never
written, so every later run repeated the same capped read. A window
dense enough to fill a page with its own history stalled sampling for
good.

The read is now paged. Each page drops its newest bucket, which the
limit may have split, and the next page re-reads that bucket whole, so
the cursor advances by at least one interval per page. Only a bucket
that fills a page on its own is unsamplable, and that is reported
rather than silently truncated.

Page size is a constructor argument so a test can reach the cap without
50,000 rows.

fix(realtime): sweep open connections once per worker exit

Swoole re-runs the exit hook until the worker's loop is empty, so the
sweep ran on every call: one shutdown wrote a few hundred warnings and
re-closed connections that were already closing. It now runs once and
the later calls let the closes it started drain.

Found running the fix locally against a real stack.

test(usage): assert sampled output, not the queries behind it

One test inspected the read's query methods and time bounds, and
another counted event reads, both of which pin how the fold fetches
rather than what it samples. The window boundary they guarded is
already observable: an open exactly one window back ages out of the
level, and one inside it still counts.

Coverage is unchanged -- with the clock pinned, the carried fold still
fails six of the seven tests, and the pre-paging read still fails the
dense-paging one.

fix(realtime): give the exit drain the whole shutdown budget

worker holding thousands of connections: whoever stops the process caps
the drain anyway -- a Cloud pod leaves ~10s after its 20s preStop, out
of a 30s grace period -- so a lower value only cuts the drain short and
strands the rest.
