fix(storage): stop rejecting clean uploads the scanner could not scan

php-clamav 2.0.0 sizes every INSTREAM frame at the fixed chunk length
rather than the bytes actually read, and loops on !feof(), which is only
true after a read has hit the end. A file is therefore sent roughly
doubled and NUL-padded, and the framing desyncs: ClamAV reads file
content as a length prefix and answers with an error rather than a
verdict.

  file 1000 bytes -> 2000 bytes sent
  file 8192 bytes -> 16384 bytes sent
  file 9192 bytes -> 16384 bytes sent

2.0.1 fixed the framing, 2.0.2 added a result type. Both are taken here.

The second half matters on its own. fileScanInStream() answered false for
a detection and for a scan that never happened alike, and this acted on
the second as the first: it deleted the upload and returned 403 "The
uploaded file is invalid". Someone whose file was fine was told it was
not, and the file was gone. A detection now keeps its 403 and its delete;
a scan that failed returns 500 with the daemon's own reply and leaves the
upload alone.

This is live on main: `Tests / E2E / Antivirus` fails 2 runs in 19 with
`INSTREAM: Size limit reached, (requested: 247036)` -- a length read out
of file bytes -- surfacing as `403 matches expected 201`.

Verified against clamd 1.4 with a custom signature rather than EICAR, and
StreamMaxLength lowered to force a refusal:

  clean file                     clean      -
  detected (custom signature)    infected   Appwrite.Test.Marker.UNOFFICIAL
  oversized                      failed     -

No E2E covers the failed-scan branch. Reaching a reply-level refusal
needs StreamMaxLength below APP_LIMIT_ANTIVIRUS, and they default to 25M
and 20M, so the only way to trigger it in that lane would be to
reconfigure the shared daemon and stop it testing the configuration we
ship. The classification itself is covered in php-clamav, where the tests
fail on the previous semantics with the size refusal reporting 'infected'
where 'failed' is expected.

fix(account): keep the current session through the OAuth2 token flow

The OAuth2 redirect handler deleted the caller's current session for
both flows. That is right for createOAuth2Session, which replaces it
with the session it creates and sets the cookie, so the browser stays
signed in. createOAuth2Token creates no session there; the app exchanges
the returned token through createSession later. Deleting the current
session in that flow signed the caller out until the exchange, so a
signed-in user connecting a provider landed on the success URL as a
guest and any auth guard bounced them before the token could be used.

Delete the current session only when the flow creates a replacement.
In the token flow the identity is still attached to the signed-in
account, the existing session stays valid, and createSession adds a
session next to it.

- Document the behavior on createOAuth2Token.
- E2E: token flow while signed in keeps the session, the exchange adds
  a second one, and the session flow still replaces the current one.

fix(abuse): lease the rate limiter's Redis connection from a pool

The `timelimit` resource built its TimeLimit on a process-global `\Redis`
created with pconnect, so every coroutine in a worker shared one socket.
2.1.0 moved the HTTP server to Mode::HYPERLOOP_B, which sets
SWOOLE_HOOK_ALL, making that socket coroutine-aware. Concurrent abuse
checks in one worker then hit:

    Swoole\Error: Socket#16 has already been bound to another coroutine#14
      at Abuse/Adapters/TimeLimit/Redis.php:49

and the worker exited with status 255. Under 2.0.0 there were no hook
flags, so the same shared socket merely blocked the worker and serialized.

Reproduced on the 2.1.0 image with 64 concurrent unauthenticated uploads:
56 of 64 failed at the connection level and both HTTP workers exited
repeatedly, while Docker reported the container healthy the whole time.

Abuse gets its own pool rather than sharing `lock`, whose leases are held
for the whole guarded callback -- for storage chunk uploads, across the
transfer. The lease spans the callback because one TimeLimit issues
several round trips. Call sites return their decision instead of throwing
inside the lease: the pool treats a thrown exception as a failed lease and
reconnects the socket before returning it.

Four of the seven `timelimit` injections were never called; removed.

fix(realtime): run abuse checks through the leased time limiter

The `timelimit` resource takes a callback now, and realtime resolved it
from the shared container and called it with three arguments, so every
websocket connection reaching the abuse check raised an ArgumentCountError.

Both realtime abuse sites move onto the pooled lease. That also retires
`getRedis()` and `getTimelimit()`, which cached a `pconnect` handle in the
coroutine context: the cache was per coroutine but phpredis returns the
same persistent socket per process, so realtime shared one connection the
same way the HTTP path did. Nothing else referenced either helper.

fix: stop MariaDB healthcheck from depending on the entrypoint healthcheck user

The healthcheck.sh --connect probe authenticates as the healthcheck@localhost
user that the official MariaDB entrypoint only creates during first init or
mariadb-upgrade. Volumes initialised by older images, or left with a stale
.my-healthcheck.cnf by an interrupted upgrade, never get that user, so the
container is permanently unhealthy and every service that depends on it with
condition: service_healthy fails to start during install and upgrade.

Ping as root over TCP instead: root always exists in Appwrite volumes, and the
temporary server used during init/upgrade runs with --skip-networking so the
probe cannot pass early. Also add a restart policy matching the other database
services.

Console organization creation is serialized behind the

fix(builds): repoint rules before marking a deployment active

The Jobs worker activated a build by setting the resource's deploymentId
first and then walking the platform rules to point them at the new
deployment. Clients learn that a deployment went live by polling the

feat(notifications): let a notification name the team it belongs to

The notifications collection can only describe a notification about something inside a project: projectId and projectInternalId are required and every index leads with them.

Not everything we notify people about lives in a project. A domain, an organisation, an invoice and a payment method all belong to a team, and Cloud is about to start recording domain expiry mail. Today there is nowhere to put the team, so "what have we told this organisation" is unanswerable without a scan.

Add optional teamId and teamInternalId with a _key_team index alongside _key_project. Optional because a project-scoped notification has no team to name and every row written so far has none, so existing writers are unaffected.

V25 adds the columns and the index to installs that already have the collection; a fresh install picks them up from the config.

MigrationVersionsTest pins the notifications schema, and caught the new index missing from its expected list, so extend it to cover both columns and the index.

test(notifications): drive V25 over a pre-upgrade install

The assertions added with the team columns copied the attribute names and index order straight out of the collection config, then read them back through a createCollection that had built the collection from that same config. Deleting the whole V25 notifications case left all 14 tests green, so they proved the config contained what the config contained and said nothing about upgrading an install that already has the collection.

Replace them with the thing the columns exist for. Build notifications in its pre-V25 shape, run V25 over it, then store a notification against a team and read it back by team, and check a different team does not see it. Without the migration case this now errors with Unknown attribute: "teamId".

The '_key_team' entry stays in the V24 test's index list. That assertion pins the whole list and predates this change, so omitting the new index would just make an existing assertion wrong.

The fixture was built by taking the current notifications config and filtering out the two columns and the index the migration adds. Write the old shape out instead. It is a snapshot of what installs actually have, and it stops tracking the config.

Convert pool connection-count gauges to observable (#14)

* Convert pool connection-count gauges to observable

The 4 connection-count gauges (open/active/idle/capacity) are sampled
values — only their value at export time matters. Recording them on
every pop/push/reclaim was pure hot-path overhead, amplified across

* Neutralize observable gauges on telemetry adapter swap

Observable gauges are pull-based: the adapter samples the registered
closure on its own collection cycle, not when the pool acts. So swapping
to a second live adapter left the first one still sampling this pool,
silently double-emitting all four connection-count gauges. (The old
push-based gauges were immune — dropping the field reference stopped
emission since nothing called record() on them again.)

Keep references to the registered gauges and re-point them at a no-op
callback before binding the new adapter, so a swapped-out adapter stops
observing this pool. Covered by a new adapter-swap test.

fix(telemetry,pools): support multiple observers per observable gauge (#18)

Adapters cache instruments by name, and the ObservableGauge wrapper held a
single callback slot. So when several sources share one metric name (one per
connection pool: pool.connection.{open,active,idle,capacity}.count), each
setTelemetry() overwrote the previous source's callback — at collection only
the last source emitted, dropping every other pool's series. This regressed
pool dashboards after pools 1.0.6 moved these gauges from push to observable.

Make the shared instrument accumulate callbacks instead of overwriting: the
OpenTelemetry (and Test) wrapper keeps a list and invokes all of them at
collection. observe() keeps its void contract. The Test adapter now caches
observable gauges by name, mirroring OpenTelemetry, so the multi-source case
is exercised — this is why the original tests passed.

Pool drops the gauge bookkeeping it no longer needs. The only adapter swap
that happens is the constructor's NoTelemetry -> live rebind, which is
harmless (the dead gauges live on a different adapter instance and are never
collected), so no per-pool deregistration is required.

Adds a two-pool regression test asserting both pools emit distinct series.

Introduce an injected onConnect authenticator so the broker stays free of any
Appwrite dependency (extractable to utopia-php/mqtt). CONNECT resolves an
identity via the authenticator and rejects with CONNACK 0x87 on failure; the
AUTH packet re-verifies on reauth and enforces the projectId matches the one
pinned at CONNECT, so a connection cannot switch tenants. Fold the CONNECT and
AUTH property blocks into one reader, and name the response/reason-code bytes as
constants instead of raw hex.

The MQTT analog of app/init/realtime/connection.php, without the HTTP surface

User::sessionVerify — the same transport-agnostic domain logic HTTP uses.

feat(mqtt): authenticate by auth method and support JWT credentials

Thread the CONNECT Authentication Method through the authenticator seam

fix(messaging): keep a single SMTP recipient in the To header

Every SMTP send moved its recipients into BCC and emptied the To list. The
default recipient the comment promised was dropped when the messaging Email
message stopped taking one, so nothing was left to occupy the field, and the
renderer omits a header whose value renders empty. Mail arrived with no To at
all, which clients show as a missing recipient and some MTAs score as spam.

Hiding recipients from each other only matters when there is more than one, so
restrict the rewrite to batches. A lone recipient keeps a real To header, and
multi-recipient sends still disclose nothing.

No placeholder is put back in To: the SMTP envelope unions to, cc and bcc into
the forward paths, so any address there would receive a copy of every batch and
be counted as delivered.

one.

test(messaging): authenticate against the mail container

fix(deletes): keep a recreated domain's certificate when its old rule is deleted

Rule deletion is queued, so the deletes worker can run after the same
domain has been added again under a new rule. It then tore down the
provider certificate and routing that the new rule had just set up, and
dropped the certificate record the new rule may reference, leaving the
recreated domain without TLS until someone retried it by hand.

Only clean up the provider and dispatch RuleDeleted when no rule holds
the domain any more, and only delete the certificate record when no rule
references it. Pass the rule's domain type to the provider so cleanup
reaches the provider that issued the certificate.

fix(deletes): fall back to the rule type when the resource type is empty

API rules persist `deploymentResourceType` as '' (the attribute default),
and `Document::getAttribute()` only substitutes its default for an
absent attribute, so the fallback to `type` never fired for them once
the rule had been through the database.

Build the test collections from the canonical definitions so the schema
the worker is tested against cannot drift from production, and seed the
API case with the persisted default so the fallback is exercised on real
data.

fix(deployments): canonicalize the root directory an artifact indexes into

`providerRootDirectory` reached the jobs-service through
`trim($subdir, '/')`, which strips slashes but not dots. `docs`, `docs/`
and `/docs` all canonicalized to `docs`, while `./docs` survived verbatim
as an artifact subdir naming a path segment that does not exist in the
extracted tree. `.` and `./` were worse: they collapsed to a non-empty
`.`, so the repository-root case emitted a subdir instead of omitting one.

Canonicalize on the consume side, in `Deployments::rootDirectory()`. Every
remote-source build funnels through `submit()`, so one choke point covers
new writes, rows already holding `./docs`, webhooks, duplicates and
templates without a migration.

Drop whole `.` segments rather than trimming the character. The builds
worker's `ltrim($path, '.')` turned `.github` into `github` — a silent
wrong-directory build — and left `../etc` traversal intact. Both worker
call sites now share the canonicalizer, and the jobs-service hand-off
passes the canonicalized value instead of re-reading the raw attribute,
which also closes a mismatch where the template push committed at a
space-stripped path but sent the space-bearing one.

`..` segments are dropped rather than resolved, so a subdir cannot escape
the tree it indexes into.

fix(vcs): record the root directory on webhook deployments

The shared deployment document carried every other `provider*` field but
not `providerRootDirectory`, so a push-triggered deployment persisted an
empty root directory. The build itself was correct — the root directory
is passed separately — but duplicating such a deployment reads the value
back off the source document, so a redeploy silently built from the
repository root.

The trait is shared by GitHub, GitLab, Gitea, Bitbucket and Origin.

fix(deployments): refuse a root directory that leaves the repository

Dropping `..` segments made `docs/../x` build `docs/x`, which is neither
the directory the caller named nor the one POSIX would resolve — and if
both exist, the wrong application deploys with no warning. Resolving the
segment instead would let the subdir climb out of the tree it indexes
into.

Refuse the path instead. The failure is the owner's to fix, so it joins
the refused-variable-key case in carrying its reason into the build log
rather than a generic internal error.

test(vcs): cover a nested root directory through push and duplicate

Builds a function from './docs/nested/' — the form the console's
directory picker writes — over the Gitea suite, the only live-VCS suite
CI boots.

Covers both halves observably: the push-created deployment must execute
the nested entrypoint, and duplicating it must reach 'ready'. A duplicate
reads the root directory back off the source deployment, so a regression
that stops persisting it builds from the repository root, where the
auto-init README is the only file and no entrypoint exists.

test(vcs): prove the persisted root directory through the duplicate build

The deployment response model does not expose providerRootDirectory, so
reading it off the body asserted on a key that is never returned.

Duplicating the push-created deployment proves the same thing through
behavior: the duplicate reads the root directory back off the deployment
it copies, so it only reaches 'ready' if the push persisted one. Also
deploy explicitly before pushing, so the nested entrypoint is observed
executing on a deployment the test activated rather than one it assumed
was active.

fix(mongo): initialise the data directory off the port the server binds

On a fresh volume the standard mongo entrypoint creates the users and runs
/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d against a temporary mongod on 127.0.0.1:27017, stops
it with `mongod --shutdown`, and execs the real server on 0.0.0.0:27017.

That handover is unsynchronised. `mongod --shutdown` returns once the server it
signalled clears <dbpath>/mongod.lock, but a mongod releases its listening socket
only when the process exits, several steps after the lock goes. The real server
binds about a millisecond after it starts, so whenever the tail of the temporary
server's shutdown outlasts the handover it gets

  Error setting up transport layer ... 0.0.0.0:27017 :: caused by ::
  setup bind :: caused by :: Address already in use

and exits 48. The container goes with it, so `docker compose up -d --wait` fails
every service that depends_on mongodb and the lane reports "dependency failed to
start: container appwrite-mongodb is unhealthy" having run no tests at all. Run
34374778610 lost Tests / E2E / PostgreSQL (shared) / Locale that way: the
temporary server reached "Dropping the scope cache for shutdown" and had still
not logged "Now exiting" when the real one tried to bind 1.08s later.

Initialise here instead, on a port the real server never binds, and wait on the
process rather than on its lock file. The standard entrypoint then finds an
initialised directory, starts no second server and execs straight through, so
mongod is still PID 1 on every boot including the first. The users are unchanged:
root@admin with the root role, and _APP_DB_USER@admin with readWrite on
_APP_DB_SCHEMA.

mongo-init.js moves out of /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d, because anything left in
there sends the standard entrypoint back to the temporary server regardless of
the data directory. mongo-init-replicaset.sh goes too: unreferenced since the
healthcheck took over replica set initiation, and written to be mounted into that
same directory.

Verified by freezing the temporary server the instant it clears mongod.lock,
which is what a loaded runner does to its shutdown tail: the current entrypoint
exits 48 on every attempt, this one serves. Also five `docker compose down -v` /
`up -d --wait` cycles on a fresh volume, and a restart on an initialised one.

fix(mongo): make first-boot initialisation resumable

that file meant a first boot interrupted between the two -- a killed container,
a failed mongosh -- came back with authentication on and nobody to authenticate

skippable so a resumed pass finishes whatever did not happen. Checked against a
data directory seeded with no users and one seeded with root but not the

directory the released entrypoint initialised is picked up unchanged, replica

feat(mqtt): add the keep-alive timing wheel and connection state

KeepAlive is a hashed timing wheel: connections bucket by their deadline second,
schedule() returns the slot the caller stores on the Connection, drain() returns
every fd due at or before a tick, and remove() drops a fd (and its emptied
bucket). Connection carries keepAlive/expiresAt/wheelSlot and touch() pushes the
deadline to keepAlive x MULTIPLIER; the CONNECT handler parses the keep-alive it
used to skip.

test(mqtt): cover the keep-alive wheel and reaper

Unit-test the wheel (schedule/drain/remove, coarse-tick range drain, past
deadline, emptied-bucket cleanup) and Connection::touch. E2e: a silent client is
reaped past its keep-alive, and an actively pinging client survives a full reaper
interval (also exercising PINGREQ/PINGRESP). Adds MqttSubscriber ping/awaitClose
and a keepAlive connect param.

Realtime, since these are app classes not overrides of the utopia-php/mqtt
package (which still provides the generic codec: Packet, Properties, Server,
Adapter). Drops the src/Utopia/Mqtt PSR-4 override; moves the unit tests too.

Also makes offline replay plan/topic-driven: replay depth comes from

the cursor TTL from the subscribed topics' expiry.

Builds one image a day from the newest CI-green commit on the active

Resolves the build rather than trusting the tip: walks back through

feat(ci): gate releases on a fresh install and an upgrade

AGENTS.md blocks a release on a fresh install and an upgrade from the
previous stable with realistic data, and CI covered neither -- there was
no migrate step anywhere in the pipeline. That gate was a person's day
per release, which is a direct incentive to batch fixes instead of
shipping them.

Both now run on release branches and on demand. The upgrade job starts
the previous published stable from the compose file and env that version
shipped, seeds through the public API, switches to the candidate on the
same volumes, migrates, and asserts the data survived -- then migrates a
second time to prove idempotency. Seeding covers the shapes a migration
is most likely to mangle: empty strings, 4000-character values, unicode,
relationships, and row permissions that differ from the table's.

The baseline comes from Docker Hub rather than git tags, because an
image nobody can pull is not an upgrade anyone can perform.

version number, and tests/unit/Release/MetadataTest.php fails when they

The task also refuses to map a patch to a new migration class: a fix

The upgrade gate read the previous stable out of Docker Hub's 100 most

test(account): cover real Google and Apple ID token payloads

The ID token e2e tests all mint minimal claim sets, so nothing exercised
the payloads the providers actually send. Two shapes were untested:

- Google's full claim set, where `azp`, `hd`, `at_hash`, `given_name`,
  `family_name` and `locale` ride along with the claims the flow reads,
  and `name` and `picture` have to reach the account and its identity.
- Apple's, where `email_verified` and `is_private_email` arrive as the
  strings "true" rather than JSON booleans, the nonce is carried as the
  SHA-256 of the raw value, and no `name` or `picture` claim is ever
  sent, so the name falls back to the request parameter and the identity
  is left without a photo.

`Create.php` already handles both, filter_var()-ing the string booleans
and defaulting the photo to empty; this pins that behaviour down.

`iss`, `aud` and `picture` stay pointed at the mock provider so the
tokens verify against the mock JWKS and the avatar is fetchable in CI.
Every other claim is the provider's own shape.

keeping only the handful of claims the identity models. Clients that want
anything else — Google's `locale`, say, which is useful for picking a UI
language but not worth an attribute of its own — have no way to read it
back short of another round trip to the provider.

Keep the raw token on the identity instead, and hand it back on the
Identity model so clients can decode whatever claims they need.

- `providerIdToken` on `identities`, encrypted at rest like the access
  and refresh tokens beside it, and sized to match. The ID token param
  caps at 8192 characters, so 16384 leaves room.
- V25 creates the attribute alongside `photo`, the same way.
- Written on identity creation and refreshed on every subsequent
  sign-in: the stored token expires within the hour and its claims may
  have changed since.

Only the native flow stores one. The browser OAuth2 flow never sees an
ID token, so its identities leave the attribute empty.

feat(auth): make the pwned lookup adapter driven

The breach lookup moves out of the validator and behind an adapter, so a
server can choose who answers the question.

- `hibp` keeps the current behaviour: the public Have I Been Pwned range
  API with k-anonymity, sending only the first five characters of the
  SHA-1 hash and caching ranges per prefix.
- `appwrite` talks to an Appwrite Pwned service
  (https://github.com/appwrite-labs/pwned), which answers for a whole
  password. The password travels inside a short-lived JWT signed with
  `_APP_OPENSSL_KEY_V1`, so it is only appropriate for a service on your
  own network, and in exchange the service caches and can front a
  detector of its own choosing.

`_APP_PWNED_PASSWORDS_ADAPTER` picks the adapter and defaults to `hibp`.
`_APP_PWNED_PASSWORDS_ENDPOINT` now defaults to empty and falls back to
whichever address the chosen adapter ships with. An unknown adapter name
fails loudly at request time rather than quietly falling back.

`PasswordPwned` keeps the policy decisions and delegates the lookup, so
its unit test no longer needs an HTTP double. Each adapter has its own
test next to it.

fix(functions): publish a deployment as ready only once it is executable

finalize() wrote the terminal status onto the deployment before it pointed
the resource at that deployment, so between those two writes the API
reported a build as ready while the function still had an empty
deploymentId. A client that polled for ready and immediately executed got
404 DEPLOYMENT_NOT_FOUND from POST /v1/functions/:functionId/executions.

The window is wide enough to hit in practice because activate() walks every
matching platform rule before it writes deploymentId, and is what makes
testDeploymentBuildOutputIsServedFromTheBuildsDevice flaky in the s3 group.

Split the terminal write in two so the status flip is the last thing
finalize() does: build metadata and the latestDeployment pointer land first,
then activation, then the status. Both writes keep the notEqual('canceled')
guard, so a concurrent cancel still wins. latestDeploymentStatus is
refreshed after the flip rather than before it, so a client that
force-activates on seeing ready cannot race BUILD_NOT_READY.

The e2e probe now asserts the invariant in the same iteration that first
observes ready, throwing Critical so assertEventually cannot retry the
failure away.

The key is emitted on every CustomId parameter with the single constant
value "ID.unique", so it carries no information beyond "this validator
was CustomId", and an audit found no consumer reading it: not the SDK
generator, not vibes, not the console, MCP, or the Terraform provider.

Vibes classifies creatable resource IDs from the schema description
instead, matching /choose a custom … id|generate a random id|ID.unique\(\)/
in isCreatableIdSchema(), and treats every path and query parameter as an

already matched by that regex and 7 of the remaining 8 are path parameters
vibes excludes by rule, so removing the extension changes no consumer
behaviour.

what OpenAPI cannot express, and a constant-valued flag with no reader
does not qualify.

following those fields builds the wrong request.

and is no longer emitted as a security scheme. Examples keep configuring the

example still renders `setProject(...)`.

fix(deletes): simplify the recreated-domain certificate guard

The certificateId lookup could never match a rule. Every rule creation site
persists an empty certificateId, the only writer of a real id is the
certificates worker updating the single rule it processed, and _key_domain is
unique, so a certificate document is 1:1 with a rule. The rule's own row is
always gone before the worker runs. That left an unindexed scan of rules on
every deletion, guarding a delete it always permitted. Restore the
unconditional cleanup: a replacement rule allocates its own certificate
document, so keeping the old one orphans a renewal that reschedules forever.

Derive the domain type the way the issuing sites do. deploymentResourceType
defaults to '' and is always persisted, so the default argument never fires
and an API rule issues under ''. Falling back on empty instead sent the delete
to 'api', a different bucket than the one the certificate was issued under.

test(queue): prove the in-memory fake serves a batched receive

Review flagged rightPopMany() for ignoring $timeout. It does, as every
pop in this fake does -- nothing here blocks, an empty pop yields, and

not a fix.

The real defect underneath was quieter: each message after the first went

takes the company it finds. The rest now comes straight off the list.

test(queue): assert the batched sibling at the worker boundary

The previous test's subject was the fake itself -- it drove
receiveBatch() directly and asserted the broker's return. Review called
that implementation-coupled and it is: a test whose subject is a fixture
proves the fixture, not the worker.

What matters about batching here is the boundary between queues. Batching
changes how many messages one receive claims, not how many run at once,
so the way it could go wrong is by occupying slots another queue is
serialised by, or by losing or duplicating what it claimed. The combined
-mode case now runs its parallel sibling batched and asserts what came
out: every message once, databases still serial, the cap still the cap.

Worth knowing what this cannot see: a batch size that is ignored outright
behaves identically at this boundary, because the whole point of a batch
is fewer round trips and nothing else. Claiming is not observable from
out here.

fix(agents): send requests through a reused utopia-php/client

utopia-php/fetch's cURL adapter registers non-static closures on the handle, which binds the adapter and leaves CurlHandle -> closure -> adapter -> handle as a reference cycle. Every adapter built a fresh fetch client per request, so each call left a live handle (TLS state, keep-alive socket, eventfd) until PHP's cycle collector ran. Long-lived Swoole workers rarely reach that threshold: the threats worker on Cloud grew ~50 MB/h and piled up CLOSE_WAIT sockets to api.openai.com until its 1 GiB limit. The fetch package is archived, so the cycle cannot be fixed there.

Adapters now share one utopia-php/client instance: inside a coroutine a pool of keep-alive Swoole clients, elsewhere a single keep-alive cURL client, built once per adapter with its timeout and reused across requests. Callers that already own a pooled client can inject it with setClient(). Streaming goes through the PSR-18 stream() sink as raw chunks, so the adapters' SSE processing takes strings instead of fetch Chunk objects.

Measured in the appwrite/ce:cl-2.2.0-1 image with GC never triggered: 200 agent calls grew RSS by 2.5 MB with a flat fd count, against 18 MB and two leaked fds per call before.

artifact: array_chunk() splits on the adapter's per-request limit, recipients

fix(storage): keep the APK mime type on uploads sniffed as plain zip

Content sniffing identifies a zip container from the entries at the head of
the archive, so an APK whose archive starts with res/ is reported as
application/zip while the same app built with AndroidManifest.xml near the
front is reported as application/vnd.android.package-archive. The sniffed
value is persisted as the file's mimeType and echoed back as Content-Type on
download, next to a Content-Disposition filename ending in .apk. Responses
also carry X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, so a client that trusts the
declared type over the filename saves the download as a .zip.

Fall back to the filename extension when, and only when, sniffing already
returned a generic container type. The fallback can only ever resolve to
another binary type, so a file can never be promoted from its extension to
something a browser would render and the stored-XSS property of the view
endpoint is unchanged.

Fix password pwned policy so enabled records and users/sessions block

The three policy options did not mean what they say. `enabled` alone
rejected breached passwords on sign-up and password changes, nothing was
looked up on sign-in unless `sessions` was set, and `users` refused a
sign-in rather than a sign-up.

Now each option has one job:

- `enabled` turns the integration on. Every password Appwrite sees on
  sign-up, sign-in, password change, recovery or anonymous conversion is
  looked up and the outcome recorded on the user as `passwordPwned`. On
  its own it never rejects anything.
- `users` rejects a breached password when a user signs up or sets a new
  password (`password_pwned`, 400).
- `sessions` refuses a sign-in with a breached password until it is
  reset (`user_password_reset_required`, 412).

Endpoint and model descriptions follow, and the e2e suite asserts the
new contract: `enabled=false` switches both blocking options off, and
neither blocking option leaks onto the other surface.

body was inspected, so gzip bytes named file.jar were stored as a JAR. The
extension now only resolves an ambiguous declared or sniffed type, matching the
Storage API.
